prompt: The section gives two reasons why heat and work are not state functions. One is that they depend on the path. What is the other?

choices.text: They are energy in transfer, not part of the system
They can never be measured in a real experiment
choices.why: Heat and work can be measured; the section works out the work of several compressions. They are not state functions because they are energy in transfer.

choices.text: They are always zero when the gas is ideal
choices.why: The section's ideal-gas compressions take positive work. Heat and work are not state functions because they are transfers of energy, not intrinsic to the system.

choices.text: They depend only on the initial and the final states
choices.why: That is what defines a state function. Heat and work depend on the path, and they are energy in transfer rather than something the system has.

explanation: Heat and work are energy on its way into or out of a system; they are not intrinsic to it. A gas in a given state has a definite volume and pressure, but no definite amount of heat or work.

prompt: What is a path function?

choices.text: A quantity that depends on the path taken between two states
A quantity that depends only on the starting and final states
choices.why: That describes a state function, like volume. A path function, like work, can change when the path between the same two states changes.

choices.text: A quantity that keeps the same value along any path
choices.why: Something that never changes along a path is a constant. A path function's value depends on which path is taken.

choices.text: The equation of the curve a gas follows on a P–V diagram
choices.why: That describes the path itself, not a path function. A path function is a quantity, like heat or work, whose value depends on the path taken.

explanation: Functions whose values depend on the path taken, such as work w and heat q, are path functions. Two processes between the same two states can give them different values.

prompt: The compressions and expansions in this section are isothermal. What does that mean?

choices.text: The temperature stays the same
The gas pressure stays the same
choices.why: Constant pressure is called isobaric. In these isothermal processes the gas pressure changes, but the temperature doesn't.

choices.text: The gas volume stays the same
choices.why: The volume changes in every one of these compressions and expansions. Isothermal means the temperature is constant.

choices.text: No heat flows into or out of it
choices.why: A process with no heat flow is adiabatic, a different kind. Isothermal means at constant temperature.

explanation: Isothermal means at constant temperature. For an ideal gas the pressure then follows P = nRT/V as the volume changes.

prompt: In the section's compression experiment, a 1 L cylinder of gas at 1 bar has its piston pegged in place before it goes into a chamber at P_ext = 2 bar. What is the peg for?

choices.text: It stops the piston moving while P_ext is raised
It keeps the gas temperature exactly constant throughout
choices.why: A peg holds the piston; it doesn't control temperature. It keeps the piston still until the 2 bar outside can act all at once.

choices.text: It lets the gas pressure rise slowly up to 2 bar
choices.why: With the piston fixed, the gas stays at 1 bar. The peg holds the piston so that, when it is pulled, the full 2 bar acts suddenly.

choices.text: It keeps heat from flowing out of the compressed gas
choices.why: Blocking heat is the job of insulation. The peg holds the piston still until the 2 bar outside can be applied suddenly.

explanation: With the piston pegged, the gas stays at 1 bar while the outside is at 2 bar. Pulling the peg then lets the full 2 bar act at once, so the compression happens suddenly, with P_ext > P.

prompt: In the section's experiment, a 1 L cylinder of ideal gas at 1 bar is suddenly put under a constant P_ext of 2 bar, at constant temperature. The piston shoots down and stops when the volume is 1/2 L. Why does it stop there?

choices.text: The gas pressure has risen to match the 2 bar outside
The external pressure has dropped back to 1 bar
choices.why: The chamber keeps P_ext at 2 bar throughout. The piston stops because the gas pressure has risen to 2 bar.

choices.text: The gas is squeezed to the smallest volume it can have
choices.why: A gas can be compressed further by a higher pressure. Here the piston stops because the inside and outside pressures balance at 2 bar.

choices.text: The temperature of the gas has risen enough to stop it
choices.why: The process is isothermal, so the gas ends at its starting temperature. The piston stops when the gas pressure reaches the 2 bar outside.

explanation: At constant temperature, halving the volume of an ideal gas doubles its pressure, from 1 bar to 2 bar. There the internal and external pressures balance and the piston stops.

prompt: In a sudden compression at a constant P_ext of 2 bar, a P–V diagram also shows the isotherm P = nRT/V, a hyperbola. Which pressure must be used to compute the work?

choices.text: The external pressure, P_ext
The gas pressure P read off the hyperbola
choices.why: The hyperbola gives the gas's own pressure, which differs from P_ext during a sudden change. The work is w = −∫P_ext dV.

choices.text: The average of the gas and external pressures
choices.why: Averaging has no basis here. The work uses the external pressure, w = −P_ext ΔV, at a constant 2 bar.

choices.text: The gas pressure in the starting state
choices.why: The gas starts below 2 bar, but the piston is pushed by 2 bar from outside. The work uses that external pressure.

explanation: The hyperbola is the internal pressure of the gas, but it is the external pressure that counts when computing work. The two are not the same during a sudden change.

prompt: On a P–V diagram, what shape is the area that represents the work when the external pressure stays constant?

choices.text: A rectangle of height P_ext and width |ΔV|
The area under the hyperbola of the isotherm
choices.why: That is the work along the reversible path, where P_ext follows the gas pressure. A constant P_ext gives a flat top, so the area is a rectangle.

choices.text: A triangle between states 1 and 2
choices.why: A triangle would need the pressure to change steadily along the way. A constant P_ext gives a rectangle of height P_ext.

choices.text: A single line with no area under it
choices.why: The volume changes, so the area has a width as well as a height. A constant P_ext gives a rectangle of area P_ext × |ΔV|.

explanation: As long as P_ext is constant, w = −P_ext ΔV, which is a height P_ext times a width ΔV on the diagram. The work is therefore the area of a rectangle.

prompt: An ideal gas is compressed isothermally from state 1 at 1 bar to state 2 at 2 bar. On a P–V diagram, the reversible work is the area under the isotherm, and the work of a sudden compression at P_ext = 2 bar is the area under a flat line at 2 bar. Why is the second area larger?

choices.text: The isotherm lies below 2 bar until it reaches state 2
The sudden compression spans a larger change in volume
choices.why: Both compressions go from state 1 to state 2, so their widths are the same. The flat line is higher, since the gas pressure is below 2 bar until the end.

choices.text: The isotherm lies above 2 bar for most of the way
choices.why: The gas starts at 1 bar and only reaches 2 bar at state 2. So the isotherm runs below the flat line at 2 bar.

choices.text: The sudden compression ends at a higher temperature
choices.why: Both compressions are isothermal and end in the same state. The difference comes from the gas pressure being below 2 bar along the way.

explanation: Along the isotherm, the gas pressure climbs from 1 bar at state 1 to 2 bar at state 2. The flat line sits at 2 bar the whole way, so it encloses more area.

prompt: The sudden and the reversible compressions both take the gas from state 1 to state 2. According to the section, what is the key difference between them?

choices.text: The sudden one has P_ext > P; the other keeps P_ext = P
The sudden one ends at a higher temperature than the other
choices.why: Both are isothermal and end in the same state 2. The difference is that P_ext > P in the sudden one, while P_ext = P in the reversible one.

choices.text: The reversible one squeezes the gas into a smaller volume
choices.why: Both end at state 2, with the same volume. What differs is the pressure balance: P_ext > P in the sudden one, P_ext = P in the reversible one.

choices.text: The sudden one is done with a gas that doesn't behave ideally
choices.why: The same ideal gas is used in both. The difference is that the sudden one has P_ext > P, while the reversible one keeps P_ext = P.

explanation: Pulling the peg suddenly sets P_ext above the gas pressure, which then struggles to catch up. In the reversible compression, P_ext = P at all times.

prompt: How does the section describe a reversible path?

choices.text: A series of states at rest, always with balanced forces
A path in which the forces balance only at the very end
choices.why: That describes an irreversible path. Along a reversible one the forces balance at every step, so the system passes through states at rest.

choices.text: Any path that brings the system back to where it started
choices.why: Returning to the start makes a cycle, which can be reversible or not. A reversible path is a series of states at rest, with balanced forces.

choices.text: A path that is carried out as quickly as possible
choices.why: Speed works against reversibility; a sudden change is irreversible. A reversible path goes through states at rest, with the forces always balanced.

explanation: A reversible path follows a series of states at rest, with the forces allowed to balance at all times. In an irreversible one, the forces only balance at the very end.

prompt: The section compares its two compressions to falling off a cliff and to gently sliding down a hill. Which compression is like falling off the cliff?

choices.text: The sudden one, made by pulling the peg
The reversible one, done in tiny steps
choices.why: Tiny steps with balanced forces are the gentle slide down the hill. The cliff is the sudden, irreversible compression.

choices.text: Neither, since both end in the same state
choices.why: Ending in the same state doesn't make the paths alike. The sudden compression, with the forces out of balance, is the cliff.

choices.text: Whichever one needs less work
choices.why: The reversible compression needs less work, and it is the gentle slide. The sudden, irreversible one is the cliff.

explanation: The sudden compression is irreversible: the forces are out of balance until the end, like a fall. The reversible one moves through balanced states, like a gentle slide down a hill.

prompt: Which of these compressions comes closest to being reversible?

choices.text: Raising P_ext in tiny steps, always just matching P
Pulling a peg so that 2 bar acts on the piston at once
choices.why: That is the section's sudden, irreversible compression, with P_ext far above P. A reversible one keeps P_ext equal to P at every step.

choices.text: Dropping a heavy weight onto the piston in one go
choices.why: A sudden large push makes P_ext much larger than P, so the forces are out of balance. A reversible compression goes in tiny steps with balanced forces.

choices.text: Using two quick steps, first at 1.5 bar and then at 2 bar
choices.why: Two steps are closer than one, but P_ext still starts each step above P. Reversible means infinitesimally small steps with P_ext = P.

explanation: A reversible compression proceeds in infinitesimally small steps with P_ext = P at every stage, so the gas passes through states at rest. Any sudden jump in P_ext makes the process irreversible.

prompt: Which expression gives the work for a reversible isothermal change of an ideal gas from volume V_1 to V_2?

choices.text: w = −nRT ln(V_2/V_1)
w = −P_ext(V_2 − V_1)
choices.why: That is the work at a constant external pressure, the sudden path. Along the reversible path P = nRT/V changes, giving −nRT ln(V_2/V_1).

choices.text: w = −nRT ln(V_1/V_2)
choices.why: This flips the ratio and so the sign. The section's result is −nRT ln(V_2/V_1), which is positive for a compression.

choices.text: w = −nRT(V_2 − V_1)
choices.why: nRT times a volume is not an energy, and this ignores that P = nRT/V falls as V grows. Adding up (nRT/V) dV gives the logarithm, −nRT ln(V_2/V_1).

explanation: Along the reversible path, P_ext = P = nRT/V at every step, so w = −∫(nRT/V) dV = −nRT ln(V_2/V_1). For a compression, V_2 < V_1 and w is positive.

prompt: To find the reversible work, the section replaces the pressure in −∫P dV by nRT/V. Why is that allowed on the reversible path?

choices.text: There P_ext equals the gas pressure, which is nRT/V
The pressure stays constant along the reversible path
choices.why: The pressure changes along an isotherm, which is why the result has a logarithm. The step is allowed because P_ext = P, and P = nRT/V for an ideal gas.

choices.text: On the reversible path no heat flows in or out
choices.why: Heat flow has nothing to do with which pressure goes into the work. The step works because P_ext matches the gas pressure, nRT/V.

choices.text: nRT/V is the external pressure on any path
choices.why: On the sudden path P_ext is a fixed 2 bar, not nRT/V. Only on the reversible path does P_ext equal the gas pressure, nRT/V.

explanation: Work always uses the external pressure. Along the reversible path P_ext = P at every step, and for an ideal gas at constant T, P = nRT/V.

prompt: In a compression, V_2 is smaller than V_1. What are the signs of ln(V_2/V_1) and of w = −nRT ln(V_2/V_1)?

choices.text: ln(V_2/V_1) is negative, so w is positive
ln(V_2/V_1) is positive, so w is negative
choices.why: The logarithm of a number less than 1 is negative. With the minus sign in front, w comes out positive, as it should for work put into the gas.

choices.text: ln(V_2/V_1) is negative, so w is negative
choices.why: The minus sign in front flips the sign. A negative logarithm gives a positive w, matching work done on the gas.

choices.text: Both are zero, since the temperature is constant
choices.why: Constant temperature doesn't make the logarithm zero; that needs V_2 = V_1. For a compression, ln(V_2/V_1) < 0 and w > 0.

explanation: V_2/V_1 < 1, so its logarithm is negative, and the minus sign makes w positive. Work is done on the gas, as the sign convention requires for a compression.

prompt: A gas is compressed isothermally between the same two states along different paths. Along which path is the least work needed?

choices.text: The reversible path
The one-step path at a constant P_ext
choices.why: The one-step compression at constant P_ext needs more work, the full area under the line at P_ext. The reversible path needs the least.

choices.text: Every path needs the same work
choices.why: That would make work a state function. The section shows that the sudden compression takes more work than the reversible one.

choices.text: The path that is carried out fastest
choices.why: A fast, sudden compression is irreversible and needs more work. The minimum is reached along the reversible path.

explanation: The minimum amount of work needed for a compression always occurs along the reversible path. Any sudden step, with P_ext above P, adds extra work.

prompt: For an isothermal expansion between two given states, how does the work done by the gas along the reversible path compare with a one-step expansion against a constant P_ext?

choices.text: The gas does more work on the reversible path
The gas does more work on the one-step path
choices.why: In the one-step expansion the gas pushes against a P_ext lower than its own pressure, so it does less. The reversible path gives the maximum.

choices.text: The gas does the same work on both paths
choices.why: Work is a path function, so the two paths give different work. The reversible expansion delivers the most.

choices.text: The gas does no work at all on the reversible path
choices.why: On the reversible path the gas pushes against a pressure equal to its own at every step, which gives the largest work. It is the maximum, not zero.

explanation: In the reversible expansion the gas always pushes against a pressure equal to its own, so it does more work than in the one-step expansion. This is the maximum work an expansion can deliver.

prompt: A gas expands reversibly and isothermally from 1 L to 2 L. How does the work for this expansion compare with the work for compressing it reversibly back from 2 L to 1 L at the same temperature?

choices.text: Equal in size, opposite in sign
Equal in size and in sign
choices.why: One is energy given off by the gas and the other is energy put in, so the signs differ. Their sizes are the same.

choices.text: The compression takes twice as much
choices.why: Along the reversible path the two are mirror images, −nRT ln 2 and +nRT ln 2. They have the same size and opposite signs.

choices.text: The compression needs much less
choices.why: The reversible paths retrace each other exactly, so the sizes match. Only the signs are opposite.

explanation: Swapping V_1 and V_2 just flips the sign of ln(V_2/V_1). The reversible expansion gives −nRT ln 2, and the reversible compression back takes +nRT ln 2.

prompt: The section's sudden compression and its reversible compression both go from 1 L to 1/2 L at the same temperature, yet they need different amounts of work. What does this show?

choices.text: Work is a path function, not a state function
Energy is not conserved in the sudden compression
choices.why: Nothing in the section breaks energy conservation. The different amounts of work show that work depends on the path taken.

choices.text: One of the two work calculations must be wrong
choices.why: Both are right; they describe different paths. Work is a path function, so different paths give different work.

choices.text: The two compressions end up in different states
choices.why: Both start in state 1 and end in state 2. The work differs because work depends on the path between them.

explanation: The end states are the same but the work is not, so work cannot be a state function. It depends on the path, which makes it a path function.

prompt: In the section's sudden compression, a gas at 1 bar is squeezed from 1 L to 0.5 L by a constant external pressure of 2 bar. Using w = −P_ext ΔV and 1 L·bar = 100 J, what is w, in J?
explanation: w = −(2 bar)(0.5 L − 1 L) = 1 L·bar = 100 J. It is positive because work is done on the gas.

prompt: In the section's reversible compression, an ideal gas at 1 bar is compressed isothermally from 1 L to 0.5 L. For this gas nRT = PV = 1 L·bar = 100 J. Using w = −nRT ln(V_2/V_1) with ln(0.5) = −0.693, what is w, in J? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: w = −100 J × ln(0.5) = −100 J × (−0.693) = 69.3 J. That is less than the 100 J the sudden compression at 2 bar needs between the same two states.

prompt: A gas at 2.5 bar in a 2.0 L cylinder expands suddenly and isothermally against a constant external pressure of 1.0 bar, stopping at 5.0 L. Using w = −P_ext ΔV and 1 L·bar = 100 J, what is w, in J?
explanation: w = −(1.0 bar)(5.0 L − 2.0 L) = −3.0 L·bar = −300 J. The external pressure, not the gas's starting 2.5 bar, sets the work, and the sign is negative because the gas does work on its surroundings.

prompt: A gas at 2.5 bar in a 2.0 L cylinder expands reversibly and isothermally to 5.0 L. For this gas nRT = PV = 5.0 L·bar = 500 J. Using w = −nRT ln(V_2/V_1) with ln(2.5) = 0.916, what is w, in J?
explanation: w = −500 J × ln(5.0/2.0) = −500 J × 0.916 = −458 J. A sudden expansion against 1.0 bar to the same final state gives only −300 J, so the reversible path delivers more work.

prompt: A gas is compressed suddenly from 1 L to 0.5 L, with w = +100 J, and then expanded reversibly and isothermally back to 1 L, with w = −69.3 J. It ends in its starting state. What is the net work done on the gas over the round trip, in J? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Net w = +100 J + (−69.3 J) = +30.7 J. The gas is back in its starting state, yet the net work is not zero, because work is a path function.

prompt: A cylinder holds 3.0 L of an ideal gas at 1.0 bar. It is put under a constant external pressure of 1.5 bar, and the piston moves in until the gas pressure also reaches 1.5 bar, with the temperature back at its starting value. Using P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2, what is the final volume, in L?
explanation: V_2 = P_1 V_1/P_2 = (1.0 bar × 3.0 L)/(1.5 bar) = 2.0 L. The piston stops there because the inside and outside pressures balance.
